name: Nyakyusa-Ngonde
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
sweep_summary: nyak1260 Nyakyusa-Ngonde is in the catalog as fixed-dominant penultimate on Persohn 2017 sect. 2.2.3 (the catalog quote was re-verified in lines 2016-2023 and 3217-3218; the target record's catalog_quote field was empty but carries it). The single works with stress in the title, von Essen & Kähler-Meyer 1969 'Prosodische Wortmerkmale im Nyakyusa' (Festschrift Dammann, pp. 34-56, German), is a first-hand acoustic study of word prosody and CONFIRMS the classification: the accent vowel 'always stands in the penult', is acoustically strongest and highest-pitched in all 50 measured words (von Essen, pp. 34-46), and a Druckakzent 'always rests on the penultimate syllable' and shifts to the new penult under suffixation, without lengthening it (Kähler-Meyer, pp. 47-56). No open full text exists: the only scans (archive.org wortundreligionk0000erns and kalimanadini0000vari) are lending-restricted ( and search-inside could not be reached by automated download; HathiTrust and Google Books blocked the session), so the statements were recovered verbatim as highlight fragments from the Internet Archive full-text search API (60+ fragments saved and de-duplicated; raw responses; updated). Persohn 2017 cites this paper for the loss of tone and for phonetic penultimate lengthening of nouns in citation form, so it is consistent with the catalog source rather than superseding it; page-exact quotes would need a one-hour IA loan (free account) — priority medium. Two secondary snippets found on the way (OLZ 1971 review; Current Trends in Linguistics 7, 'In Nyakyusa the penultimate has stress without vowel lengthening') are consistent. all lookups used direct download/automated download against archive.org APIs.

new_statements.quote: Wie zu erwarten, erwies sich der — stets in der Paenultima stehende — Akzentvokal als der akustisch stärkste. [...] Der Vokal der Akzentsilbe trug in jedem der 50 Wörter den höchsten aller Silbentöne. [...] Im Nyakyusa liegt auf der Paenultima des in pausa gesprochenen Wortes ein Druckakzent, der die Silbe aber nicht dehnt. [...] Doch setze ich den stets auf der vorletzten Silbe ruhenden Druckakzent nur da, wo es mir der Deutlichkeit halber geraten erscheint. [...] während sich der Druckakzent auf die dann vorletzte Silbe verlagert, z.B. -boola schneiden > -booligwa
new_statements.translation: As expected, the accent vowel — which always stands in the penult — proved to be the acoustically strongest. [...] The vowel of the accent syllable carried, in each of the 50 words, the highest of all syllable pitches. [...] In Nyakyusa a stress accent lies on the penult of the word spoken in pausa, but it does not lengthen the syllable. [...] But I mark the stress accent, which always rests on the penultimate syllable, only where it seems advisable for clarity. [...] while the stress accent moves to the then-penultimate syllable, e.g. -boola 'cut' > -booligwa.

new_statements.reading: Fixed penultimate word stress: a stress accent that always falls on the penult of the isolated word, is the acoustically strongest and highest-pitched syllable, and moves to the new penult when suffixes are added; vowel length is independent of stress and the accent does not lengthen the syllable. This is exactly the catalog's fixed-dominant penultimate coding (penultimate stress), now backed by the earliest first-hand instrumental study (one speaker, 50 isolated words).

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant penultimate, non-strict) rests on an explicit statement by the leading current describer of Nyakyusa in a 2017 open-access LangSci monograph, repeated verbatim in the 2020 second edition; both PDFs are now and the quotation was confirmed verbatim (pp. 38 and 66). No fuller reference grammar or newer prosody study appears in the Glottolog list or in Persohn's own literature survey; the one instrumental study (1969, print-only) is reported by Persohn as consistent. Only housekeeping suggested: correct the locator from 'sect. 2.3' to 'sect. 2.2.3 p. 38 + sect. 3.3.8 p. 66', optionally cite the 2020 second edition, and fill the empty strength of the evidence now that the primary source is held and verified.

sources.note: First-hand instrumental study (Hamburg phonetics lab): 50 Nyakyusa words spoken in isolation by one speaker (Amon Mwakisunga; a 1957 tape of Jona Maitewele also used), measured for duration (h.s.), intensity (dB) and pitch (Hz). Von Essen: the accent vowel always stands in the penult ('stets in der Paenultima stehende Akzentvokal'), is the acoustically strongest and has the greatest duration; the accent syllable carried the highest pitch in every one of the 50 words; word structure = mid-toned light 'Vorlauf' syllables, high-toned heavy 'Schwerpunkt' (accent syllable), then a light 'Nachlauf'…

sources.citation: Persohn, Bastian. 2017. The verb in Nyakyusa: A focus on tense, aspect and modality (Contemporary African Linguistics 2). Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.926408
sources.quote: 'Nyakyusa is not a tonal language ... Instead, Nyakyusa features a regular penultimate accent. ... Every word in Nyakyusa is assigned stress on the penultimate syllable. However, words are often grouped together as a prosodic unit, in which case the penultimate syllable of the rightmost word receives a more pronounced stress.' (p. 38); enclitics: 'when they are attached, stress shifts to the new penultimate syllable' (p. 66); exceptions: 'stress remains on kaa and is not shifted to the new penultimate syllable' (p. 304).
